ety.text: From Middle English pond, ponde (“pond, pool”), probably from Old English *pond, *pand (attested in placenames), a variant of *pund (“enclosure”). Doublet of pound.

senses.d: An inland body of standing water, either natural or man-made, that is smaller than a lake.
An inland body of standing water of any size that is fed by springs rather than by a river.
To block the flow of water so that it can escape only through evaporation or seepage; to dam.
To make into a pond; to collect, as water, in a pond by damming.
To form a pond; to pool.
To ponder.
ex: Pleaseth you, pond your suppliant's plaint.

ety.text: Derived from the Old French verb estanchier, through an earlier form estanc. Unrelated to Latin stāgnum (“pond”), which influenced the change in spelling from ⟨c⟩ to ⟨g⟩.
From Middle French mare, from Old French mare, from Old Norse marr (“lake, sea, pool”), from Proto-Germanic *mari (“lake, sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri. Doublet of mer inherited from Latin.

ety.text: From Scots powny, apparently from Middle French poulenet (“little foal”), ultimately from Late Latin pullanus (“young of an animal”), from pullus. First attested in 1659. Doublet of foal and pullus. Sense “small serving of alcohol” from 19th century, both for small sizes generally and for a quarter pint specifically, from the small size.
Clipping of pony and trap, rhyming with crap.

senses.d: A small horse; specifically, any of several small breeds of horse under 14.2 hands at the withers.
ex: The pony won three times in one month and as I had backed it on each occasion I collected a ‘bank’ of over £400.

senses.d: A horse of any size.
A contraption built like a mount, strong enough to support one's weight.
A small serving of an alcoholic beverage, especially beer.
ex: 1879, “Some Queer Interviews: Interview with a Pony of Beer”, Puck, Vol. 5–6, p. 435
‘I’m on the inside track,’ said a pony of beer as it went galloping down a man’s throat.

senses.d: A serving of 140 millilitres of beer (formerly 5 fl oz); a quarter pint.
Twenty-five pounds (money).
A translation used as a study aid; loosely, a crib, a cheat-sheet.
ex: She kept the dates written down in her Latin 'pony', so she didn't have to bother about who it was.

senses.d: A ponytail hairstyle.
One horsepower.
ex: How many ponies are under the hood?

senses.d: A dance from the 1960s in which the dancer mimics the high-stepping prance of a pony.
ex: Do the monkey, do the pony / Do the slop, do the boogaloo twist.

senses.d: To lead (a horse) from another horse.
To use a crib or cheat-sheet in translating.
Synonym of crap: of little worth.
Synonym of crap: rubbish, nonsense.

ety.text: Borrowed from English poney (now pony), apparently from Middle French poulenet (“little foal”), ultimately from Late Latin pullānus (“young of an animal”).
